newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sfr current levels not hurting economy - SNB's Rich.
newsitem.headline: Sfr current levels not hurting economy - SNB's Rich.

text.p: The Swiss franc's current levels on foreign exchange markets are not harmful to the country's economy, said Swiss National Bank (SNB) chief economist Georg Rich.
"In the meantime the Swiss franc has stabilised at a level which should not be an obstacle to Swiss economic recovery," Rich said in the text of a speech.
He said that the expansive monetary policy followed by the SNB since spring 1995 had helped to bring the franc down from "overvalued" levels.
He also said the SNB's main objective is to steer policy to encourage price stability.
He noted the central bank's money supply aggregate had shown strong growth for over a year. If this trend were to continue, it would eventually lead to inflation.

"In view of the depressed state of the economy, domestic firms have no real scope to put through price increases. But we must continually be aware that monetary policy influences price levels only with a considerable lag. If we were to conduct a too-expansive policy now, the economy would, in a few years, feel the fatal effects of our mistaken decision," Rich said.
"For these reasons, we decided a monetary policy which was even more directed at currency exchange rates," he said. "These considerations will largely remain for us in the future."
He did not rule out further appreciation of the Swiss franc in the run-up to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), as European countries ready for the third step, setting up a joint currency.
"If the transition to the third stage of EMU leads to a renewed flight into the Swiss franc, we would react with easier monetary policy," Rich said.
"But we would make efforts to avoid risks. We would as far as possible steer a course which would brake the franc's appreciation, without endangering price stability on a long-term basis," he said.
He also said that it would be unwise to link the franc to the Euro, the planned EMU joint currency.
"Swiss money market rates would rise permanently to the European level, and would be determined by the European Central Bank," he said.
"As long as Switzerland remains outside the European Union, it is not foreseen that we (Switzerland) would do without our monetary policy autonomy," Rich said.
He was speaking here to the Association of Swiss Businesses in Germany. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
